extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and literary critics (writers for the English stage)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for writing and judging dramatic poetry and plays, especially regarding language, wit, plotting, decorum, and the relation of plays to contemporary conversation. Focuses on qualities a successful Restoration/English stage play should have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of Wit, Language, and Conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement of our Wit, Language and Conversation; or, an alteration in them for the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden frames the principal ideal as a general refinement: plays should show improved wit, clearer and more proper language, and reflect the improved conversation of the age. This is the overarching desideratum against which other faults are measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of Language (avoid solecisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid solecisms of speech and notorious flaws in sense; correctness in grammar and sense is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay repeatedly faults admired predecessors for grammatical errors (false syntax, misplaced prepositions, redundant words) and argues that modern writers should observe and correct such errors. Examples given include wrong use of articles, misplaced prepositions, and awkward word order (syncysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject improper or ill-sounding old words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement consists partly 'in rejecting such old words, or phrases, which are ill sounding, or improper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should prune archaisms or poorly sounding usages that impair clarity or elegance; not every old usage is valuable simply because it is old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit useful new words and phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement also consists 'in admitting new [words], which are more proper, more sounding, and more significant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce neologisms or imported terms that enrich expression or fill gaps, but do so judiciously—prefer those that prove useful and become familiar by custom rather than fashionable affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious acceptance of foreign influence (avoid over-Frenchification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not corrupt English idiom by mixing it too much with French; excessive borrowing is 'a sophistication of language not an improvement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While foreign influence can supply valuable terms, writers must avoid turning English into French; prefer English idiom and only graft foreign words that genuinely improve expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe errors first (self-correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: One testimony of refinement is that we are the first who have observed improprieties; to observe errors is a step to correcting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate sensitivity to faults in usage and sense; critical self-awareness is necessary for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent, plausible plotting (avoid incoherent or ridiculous plots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid lameness and incoherence in plots; many earlier plays were 'made up of some ridiculous incoherent story'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots should be reasonably constructed and not rest on impossibilities or far-fetched incidents. Dryden criticizes historical examples (Pericles, Winter's Tale) for implausibility and urges better-ordered plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum of the stage (appropriate action & tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the 'decorum of the stage'—actions and tone must suit the form and seriousness of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing grotesque or clownish incidents into serious scenes (e.g., clowns entering amid combats) and ensure actions (such as the wounding of women) do not violate accepted stage decorum or audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character and maintenance of chosen character
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of characters and maintaining what has been chosen to the end is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once characters and their social rank/temperament are established, keep them consistent; do not allow characters to speak or act in ways that collapse distinctions or permit the same lines to be spoken by any person in the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of wit to subject (dignity of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express wit according to the dignity of the subject; avoid falling 'from such height of thought to so low expressions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match linguistic register and cleverness to the seriousness or loftiness of the subject. High subjects require elevated diction; mixing grand ideas with coarse phrasing diminishes effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of fancy (imagination) and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A good poet needs both fancy and judgment; pleasure in fancy must be governed by judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden praises Ben Jonson's judgment and faults other writers for unbridled fancy; successful drama pairs imagination with the craft of ordering, pruning, and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid meanness of expression and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid meanness of expression (low, coarse diction) and meanness of thought in tragedy and more elevated forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While low characters may use low wit, principal characters and tragic scenes demand elevated expression; meanness lowers the dignity of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain evenness of quality across acts (avoid slumping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid initial excellence followed by fatigue; do not 'please in the first three acts' and 'sink under his burden in the fifth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain dramatic energy, coherence, and quality throughout the play—ensure later acts do not show carelessness or exhaustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-placing of words for sweetness of pronunciation (prosodic care)
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-placing of words, for the sweetness of pronunciation, is a desirable refinement (Waller introduced this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to word order for euphony and metrical sound; good prosody enhances the theatre experience and signals craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected Latinisms or learned affectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using Latinized or affected idioms (e.g., 'ports' for 'gates') that sacrifice English idiom to pedantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor natural English phrasing over artificial insertions that prioritize learnedness over clarity and native idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gross faults noted in predecessors (specific errors as anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific recurring faults—redundant words, false constructions, misplaced prepositions, syncysis, wrong articles—should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden gives many concrete examples of earlier writers' errors; use these as anti-patterns to be corrected in new writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasteful innovation of meaning (grafting new senses onto old words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve language by applying received words to new signification (a legitimate way of refining language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like Horace, craft may 'dixeris egregie, notum si callida verbum reddiderit junctura novum'—innovate meaning where graceful and effective, but with taste and elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect contemporary conversation and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should imitate present wit and conversation and be informed by the court's example and living manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of current speech, gallantry, and social manners enriches characterization and comedic raillery; plays that mirror refined contemporary conversation please modern audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour vs. true wit distinction (use of low comic devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour (comic foibles) is valuable in its place, but it differs from sharpness of conceit; do not mistake low comic 'clenches' for higher wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humour to portray folly but avoid overreliance on groveling or crude epigrammatic jests as a substitute for refined wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: A severe critic is useful (critical rigor as a quality engine)
rubrics_metrics.description: A severe critic is the greatest help to a good wit; criticism keeps a poet within bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should welcome honest, rigorous criticism—it disciplines fancy and helps preserve quality; audiences and critics play a formative role in raising standards.
